newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia diesel seen steady, despite Med export flow.
newsitem.headline: Asia diesel seen steady, despite Med export flow.

text.p: Asia's diesel prices were expected to hold steady short term with a new flow of imports from the Mediterranean and Black Sea offset by a pick up in regional demand, traders said on Tuesday.

They said about four cargoes of between 65,000 and 90,000 tonnes each were expected to arrive in East Asia in the first half of July, raising concerns that the flood of barrels seen in March and April might be repeated.
The arbitrage cargoes were sparked by lower prices in the Mediterranean compared with Asia to the tune of $27.20-$28.00 per tonne and competitive basic freight rates of about $18-$20 per tonne.

Singapore swaps prices for June were quoted at $25.20/$25.30 per barrel and July at $25.10/$25.20. Physical gas oil for end June/early July lifting was traded at $25.35 free-on-board basis on Monday, having recently recovered from this year's low of $24.90 on May 23.

China was expected to continue to curb imports in May and June because of port congestion, high stocks on the mainland and Hong Kong as well as higher domestic output as refineries return from annual maintenance, traders said.
But the import curbs were expected to absorb existing supplies by July which might prompt China to boost imports again.
India's purchase of 855,000 tonnes for July has also provided some support for the July market, traders said.

Traders said parties attracted by Asia's relative strength compared with the Mediterranean would be sensitive to signs of price weakness and so would promptly divert the cargoes elsewhere, like South America.

They also said that unlike the March-April period when cargoes from Northwest Europe and even the U.S. Gulf Coast and Caribbean were shipped to Asia, the arbitrage this time was limited to the Black Sea and Mediterranean.
The arbitrage from Northwest Europe remained shut as the West-East spread remained at a low $14.50 per tonne.
Traders said demand for prompt spot cargoes was meagre, but the focus on forward weeks produced a 20-cent contango in physical cargo prices. This was a steadying influence.
Traders said demand was coming from Indonesia ahead of the shutdown of a 200,000-barrel-per-day crude unit at the Balikpapan refinery for a month from July 10.
Indonesia bought about 2.5 million barrels in June. Traders expected July imports to rival that of April-May when more than four million barrels a month were imported.
China was seen as a wild card in July after limiting April imports to 370,000 tonnes, less than half its March purchases.

Some traders said they were concerned that Singapore's high middle-distillates stocks, which hit a four-year high of 10.54 million barrels in the week ended May 28, would stay high for a few more weeks and so pressure prices.
They said about half the stocks were cargoes from the previous arbitrage flotilla of more than two million tonnes, which have yet to be placed in the market.
"There are still lots of barrels in storage tanks in Singapore," one European trader said.
